lugar: The approaches to Moscow, Russia, from Vyazma and Bryansk, to the west, to Kalinin (now Tver), to the north, and Tula, to the south
pergunta: Why did the Blitzkrieg stop at the gates of the capital?
resumo: In the Battle of Moscow, the German offensive had lost its purpose by 1 December 1941; the extreme cold came later. What wore down Operation Typhoon.
abertura: In the first week of October 1941, the German Army Group Centre carries out Operation Typhoon with textbook perfection: six Soviet armies encircled at Vyazma, three more at Bryansk, and more than half a million prisoners. In Berlin, the government spokesman announces to the foreign press that the eastern campaign has been decided. Two months later, the same tanks are stopped about 30 km from the Kremlin, and on 5 December the Red Army counterattacks.

The explanation that circulates most has a proper name: General Winter. The German record of the time tells another story. The offensive lost its strength before the extreme cold, because of a railway that could not carry what the army consumed, armor reduced to a third and an opponent that, instead of running out, replaced its pieces. This page follows the game move by move and weighs each explanation.

lances.titulo: The perfect move: Vyazma and Bryansk
paragrafos: On 6 September 1941, Directive No. 35 gives priority back to Army Group Centre, halted east of Smolensk since August. Guderian's 2nd Panzer Group attacks on 30 September; the rest of the army group, on 2 October, under autumn sun. The three panzer groups go around the flanks of the Soviet fronts and pass between them.

In about a week, six armies are encircled west of Vyazma and almost the entire Bryansk Front, three armies, in pockets near Bryansk. Franz Halder notes in his diary that the execution was "downright classical". The German count of the time records 663,000 prisoners at Vyazma and about 100,000 at Bryansk; another official German count gives 658,000 in the two pockets; recent estimates are close to 514,000. In any of them, it exceeds half a million.

It was perhaps the best execution of the German method in the whole war, and the road to Moscow was practically open. On 9 October, the German government spokesman told the foreign press that the eastern campaign had been decided. The encirclement move worked. The game was not over.

lances.titulo: The railway that could not carry the war
paragrafos: Army Group Centre lived on trains, and the Soviet gauge is wider than the European one. A German locomotive could only run on converted track; on the other lines, it depended on captured Russian rolling stock. By the end of September, fewer than 10,000 of the roughly 15,000 miles of railway in use had been converted, according to the 1955 U.S. Army study of the German documents. For the offensive on Moscow, the planners calculated raising the fuel trains from 22 to 29 per day.

On 13 November, at the Orsha conference, the armies' chiefs of staff told Halder what this meant: in all the occupied territory only 500 locomotives and 21,000 cars had been captured, about a tenth of what was needed. Winter clothing stayed stockpiled in the rear because it could not be brought forward without cutting other supplies. According to the same American study, practically none would be available for distribution before the beginning of January.

On 27 November, the army's quartermaster general, Eduard Wagner, summed it up: they were at the end of their resources in men and materiel. The army that would reach the gates of Moscow was not going to starve for courage; it was going to starve for fuel, ammunition and warm clothing.

lances.titulo: The mud, and what it really did
paragrafos: The first snow falls on the night of 6 October; the autumn rains begin on the 7th. Alternating rain and snow, and with the weight of tanks and trucks, the dirt roads turn into a quagmire. In the third week of October, the leading divisions are strung out over 40 to 50 km of road, the infantry sometimes gets ahead of the tanks, and the 3rd Panzer Group considers carrying on on foot and by horse cart.

Tied to the road, the Germans can be met head-on, kilometer by kilometer, and the T-34, with its wider track, moves better in the mud. At the end of October the army group is practically at a standstill between Kalinin and the Oka River, about 60 km from Moscow.

The weight of the mud is debated. The 1955 U.S. Army study puts it among the main reasons for the failure; Jack Radey and Charles Sharp, examining the Wehrmacht records in 2015, conclude that it contributed, but was far from the most important factor. The strongest argument against the mud as the cause comes right after: in mid-November the ground freezes, the armor moves again as if on a paved road, and the offensive stops anyway.

lances.titulo: Orsha: playing one more move with two thirds of the pieces
paragrafos: The conference of 13 November, on Halder's special train at Orsha, in Belarus, is the document that weighs most in this story, because it is from the time and because it shows that the command knew. German casualties in the east totaled 686,000 by 1 November. Of half a million vehicles, a third were unusable and only a third fully serviceable. The panzer divisions had 35% of their original tank strength. The command itself rated the 136 divisions in the east as the equivalent of 83 full-strength ones.

The arguments for attacking are also on record: the Russians seemed to be at their limit, a last blow before winter could bring them down, and the mistake of the Marne in 1914 must not be repeated, when Germany gave up a battle that was not lost. Bock did not want to spend the winter a few dozen kilometers from Moscow with the city and its railways in the opponent's hands. The army command decided to attack, with reduced objectives.
This is the decisive move of the game, and it is not a Soviet one. The player looks at his own board, sees that he has two thirds of his pieces and little time on the clock, and attacks anyway.

lances.titulo: The last offensive: to within 30 km of the Kremlin
paragrafos: The offensive resumes on 15 November, with the ground already hard. The 3rd Panzer Group takes Klin on 23 November; on the 27th, the 7th Panzer Division reaches the Moscow–Volga Canal and the next day crosses it at Yakhroma. On 30 November the 2nd Panzer Division occupies Krasnaya Polyana, about 30 km from the Kremlin — the closest point reliably recorded. To the south, Guderian goes around Tula, which does not fall.

On the Soviet side, Zhukov had spent little and received a lot: in November, the Western Front gained 100,000 men, 300 tanks and 2,000 artillery pieces, and the Stavka was forming reserve armies behind the Volga. Two of them, the 1st Shock and the 20th, went in exactly at the gap between Yakhroma and Krasnaya Polyana. Stalin held back the rest.

On 1 December, Bock writes to Brauchitsch that the belief in a Soviet collapse has proved to be a fantasy, that the troops are exhausted and that the offensive has lost all sense and purpose. From 1 to 5 December it bogs down along the whole front, and the halt orders go first to the 4th Army, then to the armored spearheads.

lances.titulo: The cold arrives later, and so does the counterattack
paragrafos: On the night of 4 to 5 December, the temperature drops to about −32 °C; on 6 December, it reaches about −39 °C on the Moscow front, according to German records. Tanks will not start, machine guns and cannons will not fire with frozen lubricant. On the morning of 5 December the Kalinin Front attacks across the frozen Volga; on the 6th, Zhukov's Western Front and the right wing of the Southwestern Front.

The opponent that was supposed to be finished had, in the Moscow sector, a third more rifle divisions, five times as many cavalry divisions and two and a half times as many tank brigades as on 2 October. Klin is retaken on 15 December and Kalinin on the 16th; in ten days the Soviets advance more than 50 km in the north and more than 80 km in the south.

On 8 December, Hitler signs Directive No. 39: the severe winter has come surprisingly early and forces the abandonment of large offensive operations. The weather explanation is born there, in the same document that ends the offensive. On 16 December he forbids withdrawals; on the 19th he accepts Brauchitsch's resignation and takes command of the army.

veredito: Typhoon did not stop because of the winter: it reached the winter exhausted. The encirclement at Vyazma and Bryansk worked by the textbook, and it was the last move that worked. After it, Army Group Centre advanced along a railway that did not supply it, through mud that tied it to the road, with tanks reduced to a third, against an opponent that replaced divisions faster than it destroyed them. At Orsha, the German command saw these numbers and decided to attack anyway. The extreme cold arrived after Bock had already written that the offensive had lost its purpose, and it turned the halt into a retreat because it found an army without winter clothing — which had stayed in the rear for the same reason ammunition ran short.

The detour to Kiev in August weighs less than the generals said after the war: it cost time and wore down armor, but it took off the board a flank of more than half a million men, and Martin van Creveld's logistical analysis concludes that an advance on Moscow at the end of August was not possible. The Siberian divisions also weigh less than the legend: there were troops from the east in the counteroffensive, but the bulk came from the newly formed reserve armies.

In chess terms, it is the player who wins a rook with a brilliant move and loses the game on the clock, because the opponent pulls another rook out of his pocket. The Blitzkrieg won the move. In front of Moscow, it discovered that the game did not end with the move.

mitos.circula: General Winter defeated the Germans in front of Moscow.
mitos.registro: On 1 December 1941, Bock writes that the offensive has lost "all sense and purpose"; the cold that paralyzes weapons and engines arrives on the night of 4 to 5 December. In November the cold helped the Germans, by freezing the mud. By 1 November the German army in the east had already suffered 686,000 casualties. The weather explanation appears in writing in Hitler's Directive No. 39, of 8 December 1941. The winter made the defeat worse because the winter clothing was sitting in the rear — and that was a supply failure.

mitos.circula: The Germans reached Khimki and saw the towers of the Kremlin.
mitos.registro: The closest point reliably recorded is Krasnaya Polyana, occupied on 30 November 1941, about 30 km from the Kremlin. The accounts of a patrol at Khimki give dates and units that do not match one another, from 16 October to 2 December; the story that the Kremlin could be seen has no record.

From 15 October 1941 the government, the general staff and the diplomatic corps were evacuated to Kuibyshev, and Stalin had a train and aircraft at his disposal. But he stayed: he declared a state of siege on 19 October and reviewed the parade of 7 November in Red Square. The account that he walked along the platform beside the train and left without boarding, on 18 October, is from the journalist Andrew Nagorski.

The numbers differ widely: more than 18 divisions from Siberia and the Far East in one count; 70 divisions from the Far East by 1 December in a broad Soviet count cited by the official history of the U.S. Army; few in the Moscow sector, in another analysis. There were Siberian troops in the defense and in the counterattack, but the bulk of the counteroffensive came from the reserve armies formed in the autumn, with many untrained troops.

perguntas.p: Who won the Battle of Moscow?
perguntas.r: The Soviet Union. The German offensive, Operation Typhoon, failed about 30 km from the Kremlin, and the counteroffensive launched on 5 December 1941 pushed Army Group Centre west: it was the German army's first major defeat of the war.

perguntas.p: When was the Battle of Moscow?
perguntas.r: From 30 September 1941 to 7 January 1942. The German offensive bogged down from 1 to 5 December, and the Red Army counterattacked on 5 and 6 December 1941.

perguntas.p: Why did Germany lose the Battle of Moscow?
perguntas.r: The offensive arrived exhausted before the extreme cold. The railway could not carry what the army consumed, the mud tied the columns to the road, the panzer divisions had 35% of their original tanks, and the Soviet Union replaced divisions faster than the Germans destroyed them.

perguntas.p: Did "General Winter" defeat the Germans at Moscow?
perguntas.r: It was not the winter that stopped the offensive. On 1 December 1941, Bock wrote that it had lost all sense and purpose, and the extreme cold only arrived on the night of 4 to 5 December. The weather explanation appears in Hitler's Directive No. 39, of 8 December.

perguntas.p: What were the casualties of the Battle of Moscow?
perguntas.r: The sources differ, and they count casualties, not only the dead. By Krivosheev's figures, the Soviets suffered 658,279 casualties in the defense and 370,955 in the counteroffensive; German reports record 174,194 in Army Group Centre up to 10 January, a figure considered undercounted.
